LEARNING PATH LESSON · ALPHABET A–Z · AGES 3–4 YEARS

Yo-yo — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson bounces: your child makes the yuh sound with a hand-bounce for every letter, becomes the yo-yo in a sink-and-spring game, and traces the letter that plants one leg on the ground.

What is this?

Y is the twenty-fifth letter of the alphabet. In yo-yo, it makes its friendly starting sound: yuh — like the start of yes and yarn. Say yuh-yo-yo with a little hand-bounce on every yuh.

What does it mean?

Y is a two-job letter — it sometimes works as a vowel — but this card does not mention any of that. Here y is pure toy box: down it goes, up it comes, and the sound rides along both ways.

What does the child need to know?

The letter is called Y; in yo-yo it says yuh, a quick friendly sound at the front of the mouth. The middle-of-word y in happy and funny borrows another sound entirely — next year’s story, not today’s.

Why this matters

A toy every relative owns makes the word instantly familiar, and be-the-yo-yo turns the sound into the game: yuh down, yuh up. The repetition is built into the toy’s whole personality.

What it teaches

Front-of-mouth glide production, sound-and-action synchrony on vertical movement, letter recognition in two cases, squat-and-stand core strength, and the gentle comedy of being a toy on a string.

Words to learn

Yyo-yoyuhdownupspring

Say this to your child

“"This is the letter Y — hello, Y! Y says yuh, like the start of yes. Say it with a bounce: yuh-yo-yo! Now be the yo-yo: stand tall... sink all the way down... and spring back up! Yuh! Again! You are the bounciest letter in the alphabet. Then trace the big Y — arms first, then one leg down."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card and wind up: this is the letter Y, and this is a yo-yo — down it goes, up it comes, all day long.
  2. Make the sound: yuh, like the start of yes. Say yuh-yo-yo and give a hand-bounce on every yuh — down, up, down, up.
  3. Trace big Y — two arms meeting in the middle, then one leg straight down to the line — and little y: an arm, a slide and a tail that dips below.
  4. Now be the yo-yo yourself: stand tall, sink all the way down slowly, then spring back up — yuh-yo-yo! Three slow bounces is a complete performance.
  5. End with a yuh-hunt: find three things whose names start with the sound — a toy yak, yesterday’s drawing, a yawn you can demonstrate — and hand-bounce the sound at each.

Look closer at the picture

Find the big uppercase Y and the little lowercase y on the card, then the yo-yo and the word Yo-yo. Ask which letter reaches the ground — big Y plants one leg on the line, little y lets its tail dangle below it.

Ask your child

"What is this letter called?" "What does Y say in yo-yo?" "Can you sink down slowly and spring back up?" "Can you do a pretend yawn for me?" — answered with a name, a bounced yuh, one full sink-and-spring and a yawn on demand.

What your child can say or do

"Yuh! Yuh-yo-yo!" Expect sink-and-spring games in every open patch of floor, y-sounds offered to yoghurt and yawns, and hand-bounces added to ordinary sentences. Being a toy is a career now. The alphabet provided.

Out in the real world

Y yo-yos through the week: yes at full volume, yoghurt at breakfast, the yard, the yellow crayon. Every yuh is the card bouncing — and any real yo-yo found in a drawer is the lesson on a string, ready to perform.

Try it together

Be the yo-yo: a grown-up holds an invisible string and calls the speed — slow sink, fast spring, wobbly middle — while your child plays the toy. Then swap: you be the yo-yo and let your child run the string. Being the caller is the better half.

Understanding check

Ask what Y says in yo-yo: a quick friendly yuh with a hand-bounce means the sound landed. A little y traced in the air — arm, slide, dangling tail — completes the toy box.

Parent tips

Keep y’s vowel career entirely off the agenda — happy and funny can wait years. If the sink becomes a drop, slow it right down; the spring is the reward, and slow sinks make better springs.

Staying safe

Yo-yo sinking happens on clear floor with soft landings — no sinking near table corners, and hands stay free to catch balance. Real yo-yos are for older hands at this age; the body version is safer and funnier anyway.

This lesson pairs with the Yo-yo flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Alphabet A–Z (Preschool).
